en: Preface to the Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment,
Written by the Dharma-Transmitting Śramaṇa Rìshān of Zhāngjiāng Chan Monastery on the Dragon Sands.
Preface to the Commentary, compiled by the Grand Master of Golden Radiance, Acting Minister of the Secretariat, Minister of the Department of State Affairs, and Chief Counselor to the Emperor.
Composed by Pei Xiu of Xian Dian Academy. Lord Pei was a native of Jixian in Hedong.

He passed the jinshi examination with the highest honors (jiake) and served as an official for the "Worthies and Upright" (xianliang fangzheng) program, eventually attaining the rank of Chancellor (pingzhang zhengxi).
His ancestor, named Xu Xuandu, had begun construction of a pagoda at Yuezhou but passed away before its completion. Later...
He took refuge with Xiao Cao, a descendant of Emperor Wu of Liang, whose name was Xiao Chao.
While visiting Chan Master Tanyan to have him observe his past causes through meditative absorption, the Master said: "Xu Xuandu has arrived late; the stupa of old remains as it was before.
Later, when the assembly requested the Master to repair the Great Hall at Longjiang, the Master said: "This shall not be my doing; three hundred years hence..."
There was a donor of robes named Zizhou Feiyi who subsequently inscribed this [vow]. It reached the Tang dynasty when he was reborn as Pei Xiu, exactly as his words had foretold.
Now, all things composed of blood and breath must possess consciousness; and whatever possesses consciousness must share the same essence—this is what is called the True, Pure, and Luminous.
It is wondrous, void, penetrating, and spiritually resonant, standing forth in solitary existence.

Because the circulation of blood and vital energy nourishes all things as being of one body, it is said that since their blood and vital energy are identical, they must likewise possess consciousness.
What is called "true purity," "clarity," and so forth, is fully present within this single body; therein, there is no increase for the sage and no decrease for the ordinary person.
Because it does not diminish, it is called "abiding alone.
Because it is the fundamental source of sentient beings, it is called the "mind-ground" (*cittabhūmi*). Because it is that which all Buddhas have attained, it is called "bodhi.
These two characters both refer back to the preceding terms such as "true, pure, and luminous," which in total constitute the mind-ground of all Buddhas and sentient beings.

Because the source of Bodhi is attained in common by all, the commentary on the Sūtra states that the "resplendent abiding-maintenance of the light of all Buddhas" is precisely the "ground of the mind" which is the pure,
awakened, wondrously luminous state of sentient beings.
Because they interpenetrate and are mutually inclusive, it is called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

In this assembly, the bodies and minds of the ten dharma realms—saints and ordinary beings alike—are mutually penetrating; principle and phenomena are harmoniously integrated, all returning to the equal fundamental limit of quiescent extinction.

Because it is tranquil, eternal, and blissful, it is called *nirvāṇa*; because it is neither turbid nor leaking, it is called "pure"; and because it is neither false nor subject to change, it is called "unchanging."
Therefore it is said that True Suchness (Tathatā) is free from faults and transcends all negations; it is called Buddha-nature (Buddhadhātu) because it protects the good and wards off evil;

it is called Dhāraṇī because it guards the good with the merit of non-loss while internally sustaining all virtues, and because it obstructs evil with the principle of non-entry while externally dispelling all errors.
The Sanskrit term *dhāraṇī* is translated here as "Total Retention" (Zongchi).
Because it is concealed and encompasses [all qualities], it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
True Suchness (*tathatā*), though concealed within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), is likewise able to encompass the nature-qualities as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
because it transcends the profound and the obscure, it is called the Land of Secret Adornment (*Guhyasamāpatti*).

Transcending the obscurity of the "Twofold Mystery" (Chongxuan), one realizes the secret realm of wondrous adornment. These ten preceding meanings are subsumed within the ultimate discourse of the Separate Teaching (Biejiao).
It encompasses all virtues in great completeness and illuminates the masses of darkness with singular brilliance; thus it is called Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue). In reality, they are all one.
It is the mind. In summary, the meanings of the preceding passages all converge upon the wondrous mind of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*).
To turn one's back on it is to be ordinary; to accord with it is to be a sage. To be deluded by it is the beginning of birth and death; to awaken to it is the cessation of saṃsāra.
To seek it through intimacy is to cultivate cessation and contemplation, concentration and wisdom; to extend it outward is to realize the six perfections and myriad practices.
Intimacy, proximity, and compliance with cessation, contemplation, concentration, and wisdom constitute the internal permeation of original enlightenment;
to investigate and expand upon cessation, contemplation, concentration, and wisdom so as to perfect the six perfections and myriad practices is the wondrous function of Perfect Enlightenment.
When these are extended to become wisdom, they then constitute correct wisdom; when they serve as a basis to become causes, they then constitute correct causes.
In reality, they are all one and the same dharma.

When extended and based upon the six perfections and the myriad practices, they become the correct cause. All that has preceded this has been accomplished through the ultimate fulfillment of self-abandonment and sustenance.
Ultimately, one realizes that from cause to fruit, all follow the regulations of a single Dharma.
To be in perfect awakening all day long yet never to have experienced perfect awakening is the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Those of the lower class are truly subject to the turning of delusion; they only turn their backs on the True and do not accord with it, like one who holds a prayer bead while begging for alms—this is what is meant by sentient beings being unaware of their daily activities.

Those who seek to realize Perfect Enlightenment but have not yet reached its ultimate perfection are Bodhisattvas; those who are fully endowed with Perfect Enlightenment and abide in its maintenance are [the Buddhas].
Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrtinirdeśa) refers to the Tathāgata.

Those who wish to realize it are the Bodhisattvas; because they have not yet severed subtle thoughts prior to reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) through the successive rungs of the stages, it is said that they have not yet attained ultimate perfection.
As for those who maintain and uphold it, only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively master it.
"Abiding" means to sustain and uphold.
Apart from Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi), there are no six realms; apart from Perfect Enlightenment, there are no three vehicles.

This reveals, by contrast, that within the nature of the six realms, Perfect Enlightenment is fully present; though one is Perfect Enlightenment all day long, one has never been [separate from] Perfect Enlightenment.

The meaning of "awakening" (jue) is that there is no separate dharma for receiving birth within the six realms; rather, it is because one is deluded regarding this fundamental awakened wondrous mind that the karmic fruits of the three realms are produced.
Thus, it is said that apart from Perfect Awakening (yuanjue), no six realms can be found. Furthermore, the stages of the Three Vehicles are not separate dharmas either;
they simply consist of awakening to this awakened mind, severing delusions, realizing the truth, and thereby attaining the Unsurpassed Way.
Without Perfect Enlightenment (yuanjue), there is no Tathāgata; yet when Perfect Enlightenment is extinguished, there is no true Dharma. In reality, these are all but one Way.
Lord Pei encompassed them all, yet did not produce a single Way outside of it.
That which all Buddhas of the three periods have realized is precisely this; that for which the Tathāgata has appeared in the world for the sake of the one great matter is precisely this;
and all the sūtras of the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of scripture are precisely what elucidate this.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time have all equally realized Perfect Enlightenment; there is no separate dharma.
It is for the sake of the "one great causal event" that the Tathāgata appears in the world, yet there is no other matter: this very Perfect Enlightenment is that one great causal event.
All the teachings of the Three Vehicles, the twelve divisions of the canon, and all the sūtras expound nothing other than Perfect Enlightenment; there is no separate dharma whatsoever.
Nevertheless, the teachings bestowed by the Tathāgata indicate that there are both exoteric and esoteric aspects to the Dharma.
The exoteric teaching refers to the sūtras, while the esoteric indication refers to the dhāraṇīs. Regarding the establishment of their meaning, there are both extensive and concise versions.

It can be roughly understood that the twenty-five wheels in the "Chapter on Discerning Sounds" are presented extensively, while the three aspects of contemplative practice in the "Chapter on Majestic Virtue" are presented concisely;
this is due to the sequence of their timing.
The *Avataṃsaka* suddenly opens the eye of wisdom without passing through the various gradual vehicles; it is early in terms of timing.
The *Nirvāṇa* directly points to the human mind without prioritizing rapid exposition; it is late in terms of timing.
This is because the capacity of those present has varying depths.
The discourse with Mañjuśrī on the destruction of ignorance is concise yet appropriate for those of profound capacity;

the discourse with Vajragarbha on the destruction of ignorance is verbose yet comprehensive for those of shallow capacity. The single dharma of the *Complete Enlightenment* (Yuánjué) encompasses and provides all eight meanings.
Were it not for those of superior faculties and perfect wisdom, who could have fully mastered this?

Therefore, within the *Gāngmíng zàng* (Treasury of Radiance), the Tathāgata spoke secretly with the twelve great bodhisattvas, manifesting and expounding it so that its subtle penetration might be widely disseminated; thus he established its principles as the fundamental source of all sutras.

If taught in secret, it is not transmitted to those who are not vessels; if communicated covertly to later generations, it is openly expounded by observing their capacities to widely benefit those of the future.
Thus, with the single seal of Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*), it is established as the fundamental principle of all sutras.
Guifeng Chan Master:
One peak of Zhongnan Mountain was shaped like a jade scepter (*gui*); the Master took refuge beneath it, and thus he was so named.
He received the Dharma from Master Daoyuan, the senior disciple of Nanyin, who was a direct descendant of Hozze.
In the western capital, Henan Prefecture, there was a temple called Heze (Lotus Pond). It was named Heze because it had proven efficacious in bringing rain through prayer;
Zen Master Shenhui resided there. He was a senior disciple of the Sixth Patriarch. Before the Patriarch had spoken, he said, "I have an object that has no name and no character.
Shenhui stepped forward and said, "It is the original source of all Buddhas, the Buddha-nature of Shenhui. The Patriarch [said], "You have stolen my Buddha-nature."
To say that it is "one thing" is not acceptable; yet you call it "Buddha-nature.

If this fellow had even a single tile to shield his head, he would have become nothing more than a follower of the school of intellectual understanding (*jñeya-vāda*). He claimed for himself the status of the Seventh Patriarch.
Below this, there was the Chan Master Faru of Zizhou. Faru went forth as the Dharma-heir of Chan Master Weizhong of Jingnan. This is the transmission of the Dharma.
Since the Seal of Suchness (Nanyin) emerged from the school of Nanquan, it is called the Southern Seal;
Master Daoyuan was a disciple of Nanyin, and Guifeng received the Dharma from Daoyuan—this clarifies the cause for the arising of the teaching.
One day, he was invited by the local official Ren Guan to receive a vegetarian meal at his residence among the assembly of monks; he sat in the lower seats and received the scriptures in order.
After shaving his head and donning the robes, he followed the assembly to the meal, sitting in the lower seats because of his young age.

While reading the *Yuanjue liao yi jing* (The Sutra of Complete Enlightenment and its Definitive Meaning), he reached the end of the scroll and was so moved by realization that his tears flowed. He returned home and reported what he had realized to his teacher.
His teacher patted him on the back and said, "You shall greatly propagate the teaching of the Perfect and Sudden. All the Buddhas have transmitted this sutra to you through their ears.

Having thus received the secret seal of the Southern School and the prophetic prediction of the *Yuanjue*, the Chan Master then read through the entire Tripitaka of Sutras and Vinaya, attaining mastery therein.
Regarding treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda-śāstra*:

the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma constitute the Tripitaka; the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* was transmitted by the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra, while the *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda-śāstra* was composed by the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa.
Thereupon, he reined in his carriage at the Dharma-realm of the Avataṃsaka and sat in meditative repose within the wondrous field of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
He investigated the nuances of the "one" and the "two," and exhausted the distinct purposes of the five teachings.
Later, upon reading the *Avataṃsaka*, it was as if the Tathāgata’s fine horse suddenly braced its reins and refused to go elsewhere, for he examined its source in detail.
Ultimately, being no different from Perfect Enlightenment, one then allows the mind to roam within the Dharma-realm and settles in meditative repose upon the wondrous site.

One investigates the Tathāgata’s single-flavor Dharma-rain; as for the five teachings—the Hīnayāna, Initial, Final, Sudden, and Perfect—because their distinctions and differences are not the same, they are said to have "diverse aims."

He then composed commentaries for it, including the *Daisho* (Great Commentary) in three volumes, the *Daishō* (Great Excerpts) in thirteen volumes, the *Ryūsho* (Abridged Commentary) in two volumes, the *Shōshō* (Small Excerpts) in six volumes, and the *Dōjō Shushō Gi* (Ritual for Cultivation and Realization in the Dharma Hall) in eighteen volumes; all of these have been circulated in the world.
While at Jikiji Temple and later while residing in his thatched hermitage, he composed these commentaries and sub-commentaries.
His exposition of the teachings was perfect; his insight into the Dharma was penetrating; his interpretation of meanings was upright, like splitting firewood;
and his entry into contemplation was as clear as holding a torch.
To analyze and explain its meaning is like splitting firewood; because the primary tenets are divided directly along the path of the axe, it is called a "section.
As the *Mao Shih* says: "Splitting firewood on the Southern Mountain—without an axe, one cannot succeed. Here, the commentary (*shu*) is likened to the axe and the scripture (*jing*) to the firewood;
entering the wondrous gate of the three contemplations is like holding aloft a torch.
Their prose reaches the ultimate limit of principle and does not allow for empty flights of rhetoric; their writing supports the teachings and does not permit frivolous ornamentation.

Their refinement of prose investigates the nature of principle rather than indulging in hollow exaggerations; their cultivation of style upholds the sacred teachings rather than engaging in vain embellishment.
He does not disparage others because of their shortcomings, and thus there is no talk of exclusion; he does not shame others because they have not yet reached his level,
and thus there is no arbitrary, impulsive discourse.
Because one does not despise the shortcomings of others due to one's own长处 (superiorities), there is no doctrine of disparagement;
nor, because one does not conceal the capabilities of others due to one's own shortcomings, is there any argument based on mere conjecture. Guifeng has distanced himself from all such errors.
Vast and expansive, it is truly the eye of the twelve divisions of the scriptures (the commentary is found within the sutras) and the marrow of the thirty-five patriarchs.
It encompasses the forty-seven masters of India and the twenty-three of the Tang dynasty, as well as Heze.
It is the fundamental basis for all living beings and the pervasive path through the three periods of time; even if there were authors in future generations, none could surpass it.
Is this not one of the four reliances? Or is it the direct gateway to the Pure Land? Why is it that its meaning and flavor are so exhaustive?
The "Chapter on the Four Reliances" in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Rely on the Dharma, not on the person; rely on the meaning, not on the words; rely on wisdom, not on consciousness;

rely on definitive teachings, not on non-definitive teachings. Furthermore, because the Tang dynasty designated the four Dharma Masters—Dharmapāla, Sengzhao, Tanyong, and Jizang—as the "Four Reliances," Pei Xiu also praised Guifeng as being one of these Four Reliances. There are some who hold this view.
"Is the Pure Land and the twelve great bodhisattvas something heard directly from the Tathāgata?
Some say (raising an objection): 'The Way has no form; those who see cannot perceive it. The Way has no fixed location; those who travel cannot reach it.
How much less can it be captured by words and letters? It resides solely within one's own nature.'"
Those who have attained awakening do not rely on words and letters, but point directly to the human mind.
How could it be adequately explained by a mere few tens of thousands of words? He replied: "Alas! It is insufficient to speak of the Way in such a manner.
Did you not say before that that which unifies all virtues and is fully perfected, which dispels the darkness of the multitudes and shines alone, is Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue)?"
Indeed, Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa) can give rise to all dharmas, and all dharmas have never been apart from Perfect Enlightenment.
Now, as for the texts of the Tripiṭaka—Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—that have been transmitted to China, numbering over five thousand scrolls, what do they elucidate?

They elucidate nothing other than precepts, concentration, and wisdom (śīla-samādhi-prajñā). And what is sought by those who cultivate these precepts, concentration, and wisdom? It is nothing other than Perfect Enlightenment. Thus it is.
To awaken to this single Dharma, one seeks it by unfolding myriad practices; yet the capacities of sentient beings differ.

Those of superior capacity do not depend on verbal explanations, while those of middling or inferior capacity are guided toward awakening through the extensive elaboration of doctrinal characteristics.
Thus, the entire Great Canon consists of the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, and this commentary is the commentary upon that Great Canon.
Since the Great Canon is itself one great *Perfect Enlightenment*, this present commentary on the *Perfect Enlightenment* is itself the Great Canon.
To explain five thousand scrolls of text with only a few volumes of commentary—is this not extremely concise?

Why, then, do you say it is prolix? When one cuts off the path of speech, stills the mind of thought, forgets subject and object, and extinguishes mental images, only then does one attain [the truth].
It certainly does not reside in verbal expression.
This concludes the response to the previous objection, which states that by using this abridged commentary to encompass the entire canon,
one may be said to save effort; if one can transcend speech and thought, forget subject and object, and realize the absence of any phenomenal marks,
this is precisely the pure realm of Perfect Enlightenment— what need is there for further verbal expression?
Alas! The realms through which sentient beings wander are the six paths. Ghosts and spirits suffer the bitterness of profound obscurity;
birds and beasts harbor the sorrow of frantic flight; the asuras are in the midst of rage, while the devas are immersed in pleasure.
To calm the mind and incline it toward Bodhi, only the human path is capable of this. If one is human and yet does not strive for it, there is nothing I can do for them. Thus it is said.
As for ghosts and spirits, this refers to those in the two realms of hell and hungry ghosts, who are perpetually submerged in the suffering of profound darkness and sorrowful lamentation.
*Rǔ* (獝) describes the appearance of birds taking flight in alarm; *xuè* (狘) describes the appearance of beasts fleeing. Within the realm of animals, beings know only fear.
Those who die in greed for life—by what means can they achieve liberation? Asuras, due to their karma of anger and their fondness for war, have no leisure to advance in cultivation.

The gods are addicted to pleasure and fail to realize the wondrous, enlightened, luminous mind; when their merit is exhausted, they fall back down. These five higher realms are not places where one can cultivate;

only within the human realm can one cultivate with a diligent heart and laborious thought, gathering [the mind] back into right mindfulness and heading toward Bodhi through hearing the Teacher’s instruction.
Xunqian previously said that although the six realms of existence are all paths of suffering, becoming a Buddha or a Patriarch likewise proceeds from the human realm;
one need only exhaust the ordinary mind and harbor no separate "sage-understanding," for if a person does not do so, there is simply nothing that can be done. That is all.
Having entered the threshold of Master Xiuchang’s domain and received the master’s manifest instructions, I have no means to instruct myself;
I shall simply praise his Dharma directly and announce it to the great assembly. All other details are fully set forth in the original preface.

Once the Duke had entered the inner sanctum of the Chan Master and received the clear and profound secret instructions, he found no way to repay this personal transmission other than by extolling the Dharma of Perfect Enlightenment;
all other matters regarding the comprehensive principles of the sutra’s thread are set forth in Guifeng’s original preface.
Please consult that for details.
